text: Research questions. A research question tells the reader what the experiment is designed to discover. A useful question names the population, the input, the decision and the evidence needed to support an answer. For a paper search tool we might ask how often the first three passages include the sentence a reader needs. The answer depends on both the questions and the collection of papers.

Paper structure. The abstract gives a short description of the problem, method and result. The introduction explains the problem in context. A methods section supplies the choices a reader needs to reproduce the experiment. The results section gives observations. A discussion explores what the observations mean under the conditions of the study. Read the original evidence before copying a number from a summary.

A document split. We divide the corpus by document before training a text model. Every window from the same document stays in the same split. If nearly identical pages appear in two splits, validation loss can look better than performance on genuinely new material. A stable document identifier helps a second researcher repeat the experiment with the same train and validation sets.

Byte sequences. Text becomes a sequence of bytes under the UTF-8 encoding. A common English letter uses one byte. Many other characters require more. A byte tokenizer can represent previously unseen words by encoding their component bytes. Decoding a sequence produced by the encoder recovers the original spacing, accents and punctuation if the bytes are joined before text decoding.

Pair counts. The tokenizer begins with a separate symbol for each byte. It counts adjacent pairs within pieces of training text and replaces the most frequent pair with one new symbol. A frequent piece contributes its count each time it occurs. A deterministic rule resolves equal counts. The order of the learned replacements matters when the model encodes a new passage.

Token boundaries. A document can contain several kinds of boundaries. Spaces separate many words, line breaks divide the displayed text, and punctuation often marks a sentence. A reversible tokenizer must preserve each original character somewhere in its output. A sequence projected back into text should preserve an extra space between words and the line break at the end of the page.

Language modeling. The language model predicts a distribution for the next token using the tokens on its left. During training the target sequence is the input sequence shifted by one position. A beginning marker gives the model a position from which to predict the first content token. An end marker gives the model an opportunity to stop sampling at the end of a document.

Attention. In attention, a token supplies a query and compares it with the keys for the available positions. A softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to one. The weighted sum of the value vectors becomes an update for the token. Different heads can learn different comparisons while reading the same input sequence.

Position. A learned position vector is added to the token embedding at each location. It gives the model a way to distinguish the first occurrence of a word from a later occurrence. When generation grows beyond the configured context length, the model reads a recent window of tokens. Evidence outside that window is unavailable to its next prediction.

Causal visibility. When a training example contains the complete sentence, its future tokens are already in memory. A triangular attention mask hides these later positions from an earlier query. One can test the implementation by replacing only the suffix and comparing the earlier outputs. The prefix should receive identical scores for every possible next token.

Residual updates. A residual block passes its input forward and adds a learned update. The attention calculation mixes information between token positions. The feedforward calculation works on the channels of each position. Layer normalization controls the scale of the vectors passed into these calculations. A final projection turns the last hidden vector into one score per vocabulary entry.

Loss measurement. A model with high probability on the observed next token receives a small negative log probability. The evaluation sums this quantity over the real targets and divides by their count. A padding label must receive no weight. Exponentiating the mean gives perplexity for the particular tokenization and text collection used in the experiment.

Gradient checking. To check one derivative, perturb the chosen parameter in both directions and recompute the loss. Divide the difference in losses by twice the perturbation size. Use double precision for this small calculation. A disagreement can reveal a missing normalization factor or an incorrectly transposed matrix in the attention calculation.

Optimizer state. A gradient describes a local direction of change, while the learning rate controls the size of an update. An adaptive optimizer records moving averages of gradients and their squares. Logging the training loss alongside the validation loss helps identify a model that begins to specialize too closely in the limited examples it has already seen.

Sampling. For text generation, the model assigns a score to every possible next token. Dividing those scores by a temperature changes how concentrated the distribution is. Restricting sampling to a short list of high scoring tokens can reduce unlikely transitions. The random seed and the exact checkpoint must be saved to reproduce a particular sample.

PDF pages. A PDF describes the placement of text on pages. The reading order returned by extraction can be surprising in a two column article. A page containing a scanned image can yield no text at all. A paper assistant should record the original page number before splitting the extracted text into short passages for the index.

Passage length. A short passage often isolates one fact, but it can split a definition from the sentence that explains it. A longer passage supplies context at the cost of extra unrelated words. Overlap repeats a few words from the end of one passage at the start of the next. The retrieval evaluation can reveal which choice serves a given paper collection.

Term frequency. A retrieval system can score a passage using the words in the question. Repeating a word in a passage raises its contribution, with a decreasing gain from each repetition. A word found in nearly every passage provides less evidence about the desired topic than a rare method name. Passage length also influences the score.

Finding evidence. To answer a question, the reader first identifies paragraphs that discuss the requested fact. Matching the terms in a question can work well for an exact model name. A paraphrase might use a different vocabulary from the paper. Inspecting the retrieved passages helps distinguish a search error from an answer-generation error.

Source attribution. A citation carries enough information for another person to find a claim. A filename and physical page number locate the source in a local collection. A short quotation identifies the relevant part of the page. The text of an answer should still be checked because a phrase copied accurately can answer a different question.

Unknown answers. A paper may report the size of a dataset without reporting the cost of collecting it. A question about cost can retrieve the correct paper while remaining unanswerable. An evaluation set should include such questions. The reader can then measure how often the system admits that the available evidence is insufficient.

Ranked retrieval. A ranked list places the most likely supporting passages first. A hit at a chosen cutoff occurs when at least one expected item appears before the cutoff. Reciprocal rank uses the inverse of the position of the first relevant item. The average across the questions reflects how far a reader usually needs to search.

Text generation. A pretrained generator has learned a mapping from text prompts to output sequences. In a retrieval application, the prompt includes the user's question and the selected source passage. The generator uses its own vocabulary and its own learned weights. A project can train a small language model separately to study how next-token prediction works.

Grounded answers. A system that expects short factual answers can require a candidate response to appear in the source passage. This makes the quotation easy to inspect. It can also reject a correct paraphrase. Recording both the rejection and the retrieved passage allows a human evaluator to decide whether the error came from generation or from the acceptance rule.

Sensor readings. A sequence of distance readings may contain an isolated large value caused by a poor reflection. A median filter sorts a small neighborhood and selects its middle element. The filter can reduce the effect of a single extreme value. An experiment should also check whether smoothing changes the timing of a genuine sudden movement.

Experimental controls. A comparison between two indexing methods should keep the papers, questions and relevance labels fixed. Changing the passage length and the language model together makes interpretation more difficult. One can change a single factor and record the difference in retrieval and answer metrics. Individual examples help explain an aggregate result.

Training records. A training record contains the seed, model dimensions, vocabulary and a history of losses. The tokenizer merge table belongs with the learned weights. If two tokenizers assign different meanings to the same integer, a model trained with one cannot interpret the other's input. Saving both items in one checkpoint prevents a common loading mistake.

Model evaluation. A held-out result is meaningful within the experiment that produced it. The number of papers, the distribution of questions and the scoring rule all affect the reported value. A small demonstration set helps catch implementation errors. A separate collection of independently written questions is needed to estimate performance for new users.

Vector search. A dense retrieval model encodes each passage into a vector. A query vector is compared with the stored vectors using a similarity measure. A lexical index compares explicit terms and can be inspected using term counts. The two approaches have different failure cases on acronyms, author names and questions written as paraphrases.

Batch construction. A language model can process several token windows together. Short documents need padding when placed next to longer examples in a batch. A label mask protects the objective from counting a prediction after the document has ended. Right padding preserves the usable prefix for each sequence in a model with causal attention.

Checking a tokenizer. A practical tokenizer test starts with a line containing a tab, two spaces and a word written in a different script. The test encodes the whole line and decodes the result. Comparing the returned string with the original catches spacing mistakes that are invisible in an example made only of isolated English words.

Reading a result. Before using a number from a paper, find the passage that describes its units and experimental conditions. A percentage for one test split can be mistaken for a result on the complete dataset. The surrounding sentence should identify both the measurement and the population to which it applies.

Evaluating a retriever. Given a list of test questions, record the position of the expected page for each one. A missing page contributes zero to reciprocal rank. Keep questions without an answer in a separate group when computing retrieval accuracy. These questions provide evidence about whether the assistant can decline to answer.

Inspecting a prediction. A language model can continue a technical sentence using a plausible method name even when the training data contain no evidence for the implied claim. Inspect the probability assigned to the observed next token for a quantitative evaluation. Use the cited paper passage when a reader needs a factual answer.

Filtering a signal. If an instrument produces an unusual single measurement, compare it with the samples on either side. A local median can remove an isolated spike, while repeated elevated samples may survive the filter. The number of measurements involved and their units should accompany a report of the result.

Reproducing a run. A second researcher needs the training documents, the exact vocabulary and the model configuration to repeat an experiment. Save the random seed and the checkpoint selected on validation data. Comparing two curves is easier when the evaluation uses the same targets and gives each token the same weight.
